title: Korean Directors Rally Behind ‘The Assassin(s)’ as Political Firestorm Turns on Its Makers
description: The Directors Guild of Korea (DGK) has come out in support of the team behind “The Assassin(s),” Hur Jin-ho‘s thriller about the 1974 shooting of fi
body:
The Directors Guild of Korea (DGK) has come out in support of the team behind “The Assassin(s),” Hur Jin-ho‘s thriller about the 1974 shooting of first lady Yuk Young-soo, as political anger over the Korean box office leader spills onto its cast and crew.

	Conservative politicians and online critics have accused the film of distorting history, and it now faces a police complaint and a fight in the National Assembly.


	“What we are facing now is not criticism or condemnation of a film, but attacks on individuals that have crossed the line,” the DGK said in a statement.
	

	The guild said the hostility had moved past questioning the film’s content and its makers’ choices, and “is targeting the daily lives and livelihoods of those who took part, and has gone as far as demanding that such a film never be made again.”

	The statement, which named neither Hur nor anyone else, accepted that every film attracts harsh reviews along with praise, and asked who could draw an exact line between fair and excessive criticism.

	“Creators can be criticized for their work, but that criticism must not lead to the collapse of the creator’s personal life and livelihood,” the guild said.

	The DGK added that its idea of a healthy creative environment includes standing beside filmmakers who want to begin again, because “the chance for that person to start their next story should not disappear simply because a film went through controversy and criticism.”

	“The Assassin(s)” opened Sept. 23. Yoo Hae-jin stars as a police inspector who witnesses the Aug. 15, 1974 shooting at the National Theater, where Yuk, the wife of then-President Park Chung-hee, was killed during Liberation Day celebrations, and goes on to lead the investigation. Park Hae-il plays the head of a newspaper’s social affairs desk, and Lee Min-ho a rookie reporter. The official inquiry pinned the killing on Mun Se-gwang alone, saying he acted under instructions from Pyongyang and Chongryon, the pro-North Korean residents’ association in Japan. Hur’s film declines to name a culprit, and its detractors argue the open ending points the finger at Park Chung-hee or his government.
	

	Controversy has not dented the box office. “The Assassin(s)” passed 1 million admissions in four days and led the Korean chart again over the Oct. 2–4 weekend, selling 412,012 tickets from 1,129 screens for a weekend gross of KRW4.07 billion ($3 million). Its running total stands at 2.23 million admissions and KRW21.9 billion ($16.3 million).

	The backlash has spread well beyond the film. Rating sites filled up with one-star scores, and the social media accounts of cast members drew abusive comments. Kim Go-eun and Lee Young-ae, who had shared handwritten recommendations, and critic Lee Dong-jin, who had reviewed the film on video, were also targeted. One YouTube film reviewer with 4.17 million subscribers pulled a video about the title.

	Lee Jong-bae, a former People Power Party (PPP) Seoul city councilor, has asked Seoul police to investigate Hur, Hive Media Corp. CEO Kim Won-kuk and writers Kwon Ki-jun and Lee Ji-min for defamation. His complaint argues that the plural title invites audiences to suspect a second culprit besides Mun. PPP lawmakers also tried to summon Hur to testify at the annual parliamentary audit, a move blocked by the Democratic Party on creative freedom grounds.

	Park Chan-wook, appearing at a Sept. 26 audience Q&A, praised the film as smartly conceived.

	In a Sept. 28 statement, the producers had said: “Nowhere in the film is any specific individual defined as being behind the incident, and the film’s hypotheses and dramatic settings are not presented as historical fact.”

	The film will open the 37th Singapore International Film Festival on Oct. 21, with Hur due to attend alongside cast members Shim Eun-kyung and Park Sung-hoon. The festival runs through Nov. 1.

	“Cinema must carry on as a place where different ideas and voices meet, even when it stirs up debate,” the DGK said. “If that freedom disappears, it becomes hard for new films and new stories to be born.”

schema.headline: Korean Directors Rally Behind ‘The Assassin(s)’ as Political Firestorm Turns on Its Makers

title: ‘Lanterns’ Finale: Hal Jordan’s Killer and Manhunter Revealed, Sinestro Creates [SPOILER], John Stewart Powers Up for ‘Superman’ Sequel
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the “Lanterns” finale, now streaming on HBO Max.

	Have no fear, the “Lanterns” finale is here.
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for the “Lanterns” finale, now streaming on HBO Max.

	Have no fear, the “Lanterns” finale is here.

	The season finale — or possibly the series finale, since HBO hasn’t renewed the show yet — wrapped up the mystery posed by the show’s premiere of who killed Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler). The episode, titled “Dirt and Stars,” also revealed the identity of the second Manhunter, and set up how John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) becomes Earth’s sole Green Lantern in DC Studios’ forthcoming “Superman” sequel, “Man of Tomorrow.”
	



	

									Courtesy of John Johnson/HBO Max
	



	The episode starts back in 2016 Rushville in the aftermath of the town’s destruction from the first Manhunter attack. Sheriff Kerry (Kelly Macdonald) finds Hal in the wreckage, and then it’s revealed that she picks him up from prison in 2026 after he’s released, waiting with beer and flowers. With their feelings for each other blossoming, the two go out for dinner, which is full of Rushville patrons with lingering hatred for Hal. Kerry defends him in front of everyone, the two later sleep together and Kerry invites Hal to her son Noah’s (Shea Pritchard) football game. However, Hal’s house is firebombed in the middle of the night, and he doesn’t manage to escape. Hal wakes up on the floor of a strange lab with Noah standing over him, explaining that he replaced Hal’s burnt skin using the same Manhunter technology that had healed John in 2016. After much speculation online, Noah is the secret second Manhunter!


	In present day, back on the planet decimated by the Manhunters, John interrogates Sinestro (Ulrich Thomsen) and learns that Noah freed the villain from prison. Sinestro reveals that he harnessed the fear-inducing gas from the planet to create a new, yellow ring for Noah. As comics fans know, Sinestro is the creator of the Yellow Lanterns, an evil group opposed to the Green Lanterns who derive their power from fear. Sinestro offers John the chance to charge his depleted ring from the sinister, yellow lantern, but Hal’s hologram stops him, and they leave Sinestro marooned on the planet.
	



	

									Courtesy of John Johnson/HBO Max
	



	Noah ambushes John when he returns to Earth, the two drive back to Rushville together. Noah reveals that he didn’t burn down Hal’s house, but says he was the one who killed him. He claims he couldn’t let Hal reveal his identity as a Manhunter and the yellow lantern to Kerry. Noah says he’s trying to overcome his violent Manhunter programming, and asks that John kills him to protect everyone from what he might do. John doesn’t answer, but lets Noah go and play one last football game for Rushville.



	

									Courtesy of John Johnson/HBO Max
	



	John joins Kerry at Noah’s game and asks her about her son being a Manhunter, convinced that she knew all along. Then, in a flashback, we see the moments right before Hal’s murder and the truth is finally revealed. After Zoe Macon (Poorna Jagannathan) saved Kerry and replaced her severed finger years ago with Manhunter technology, Kerry somehow got pregnant with Noah, who turned out to be a Manhunter like Zoe. Knowing Noah’s identity and fearing what he was planning, Hal confronted Kerry, and said they could run away and protect themselves. Kerry refused to leave, and in her fear, shot and killed Hal as he tried to reason with her by saying, “Goddamnit, I love you.” In the present, John assures Kerry that he won’t kill Noah, and instead lets her continuing raising him (as he goes on to play football at the University of Nebraska).



	

									Courtesy of John Johnson/HBO Max
	



	In the episode’s final moments, John calls Guy Gardner (Nathan Fillion) to Rushville and shows off his “unsanctioned” ring and lantern he took from Hal. John names himself the Green Lantern of Earth, in a sort of “independent contractor” role, and tells Guy to look after the stars while he protects the planet. Hal’s hologram appears and gives some last words of wisdom to John, saying he’s ready to take on the Green Lantern mantle. John tells the hologram that his final words to Kerry before his death were “I love you,” and the Hal replica repeats them earnestly back to John.

	With his ring powered up, John flies over and drops off a bag of money as restitution to the waitress Maggie (Hannah Christine Shetler) who lost her family in the Manhunter attack. He also has a touching reunion with his family back home, including his estranged mother Bernadette (Jasmine Cephas Jones). Finally, in a twist on the classic Green Lantern oath from the comics, John personalizes the phrase with an emphasis on his newfound accepting of his fear.
	

	“In brightest day / in darkest night / I embrace my fear / I’ll do what’s right / I choose this ring / I choose this fight / in service to / this lantern’s light.



	

									Courtesy of John Johnson/HBO Max
	



	While there’s no word yet on “Lanterns” Season 2, despite the show’s strong ratings for HBO, we know that Pierre will reappear as John in next summer’s “Man of Tomorrow,” James Gunn’s “Superman” sequel. It may be an awkward reunion with Fillion’s Guy Gardner, but now we know how the two Green Lanterns from Earth have decided to split up their duties. How will things go when the two heroes come face to face? How will they team up with Superman, Supergirl and the fledgling Justice League when the alien Brainiac attacks? And could Chandler have a cameo as the hologram Hal within John’s ring? We’ll have to wait and find out when “Man of Tomorrow” continues the DC Universe’s story on July 9.

schema.headline: ‘Lanterns’ Finale: Hal Jordan’s Killer and Manhunter Revealed, Sinestro Creates [SPOILER], John Stewart Powers Up for ‘Superman’ Sequel

title: J. Todd Anderson, ‘The Nice Guys’ Storyboard Artist and Longtime Coen Brothers Collaborator, Dies at 67
description: J. Todd Anderson, the storyboard artist behind films like “The Nice Guys” and “Raising Arizona” and a longtime Coen Brothers collaborator, has died
body:
J. Todd Anderson, the storyboard artist behind films like “The Nice Guys” and “Raising Arizona” and a longtime Coen Brothers collaborator, has died following a battle with cancer. He was 67. 

	His death was confirmed in a Facebook post on Oct. 3 by his “Filmically Perfect” podcast co-host, George Willeman. “My erstwhile pod-partner, J. Todd Anderson, passed away October 2nd in California,” Willeman wrote. “We had gotten together just a few months back, making plans to bring the show back as we still have/had lots of movies to talk about. While that cannot happen now, we hope to keep the website alive so that our old episodes can still be enjoyed.”
	

	His sister, Kimberly Patterson, confirmed his death to the non-profit FilmDayton, which also shared a post to social media. 


	Anderson first began his work as a storyboard artist in the late 1980s with the Joel and Ethan Coen-written comedy “Raising Arizona.” From there on out, Anderson remained a frequent collaborator with the Coen Brothers, going on to storyboard each of their films. This included “Miller’s Crossing,” “Fargo,” “The Big Lebowski,” “The Ladykillers,” “True Grit,” “Hail, Caesar!” and “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs,” in addition to their solo projects like “Drive-Away Dolls” and “Honey Don’t” from Ethan and “The Tragedy of Macbeth” from Joel.

	Beyond the Coen Brothers, he is credited with having worked on 1989’s “Twister,” 1991’s “The Addams Family,” 2009’s “Whip It,” 2018’s “The Predator,” and 2016’s “The Nice Guys.” Over his career, he was nominated for three Art Directors Guild awards for “The Tragedy of Macbeth,” “The Ballad of Buster Scruggs,” and “Hail, Caesar!” He also directed 1999’s “The Naked Man” and 2008’s “My Mummy.” 
	

	Born John Todd Anderson in Springfield, Ohio, he later attended Wright State University. The Tom Hanks Center for Motion Pictures at the university shared a tribute to Anderson on Facebook.

	“A diverse storyteller, he directed two features, published a book of his storyboards for ‘The Big Lebowski,’ co-hosted Filmically Perfect (listen below), and wrote the words and music for the pop musical ‘Nativity.’ He also generously shared his stories and knowledge with emerging filmmakers whenever they asked,” they wrote. “Rest well, JT. We’ll raise a glass to you tonight.”

schema.headline: J. Todd Anderson, ‘The Nice Guys’ Storyboard Artist and Longtime Coen Brothers Collaborator, Dies at 67

title: Korea Box Office: ‘The Assassin(s)’ Holds Admissions Lead as ‘Chiikawa’ Generates Top Weekend Gross
description: Director Hur Jin-ho’s political crime thriller “The Assassin(s)” held the top position at the South Korean box office in admissions over the weekend
body:
Director Hur Jin-ho’s political crime thriller “The Assassin(s)” held the top position at the South Korean box office in admissions over the weekend of Oct. 2–4, though Japanese animated feature “Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island” captured the frame’s largest gross revenue. 

	According to data from KOBIS, the tracking service operated by the Korean Film Council, “The Assassin(s),” currently in the eye of a political storm, led all titles with 412,012 admissions across 1,129 screens, taking $3 million and representing 23.89% of the market. By contrast, “Chiikawa” generated a weekend-high $3.2 million from 405,978 admissions across 1,055 screens to take 25.31% of theatrical receipts, finishing second on the admissions chart.
	

	“The Assassin(s)” dramatizes the August 15, 1974 assassination attempt on President Park Chung-hee and the resulting death of First Lady Yuk Young-soo. Starring Yu Hae-jin, Park Hae-il, and Lee Min-ho as investigators unpicking irregularities in the official inquiry, the production has amassed $16.3 million from 2,233,963 admissions since its launch on Sep. 23.


	“Chiikawa the Movie: The Secret of the Mermaid Island” launched wide on Sep. 30 following limited festival previews. Directed by Kei Oikawa and adapted from the manga by Nagano, the animated fantasy adventure follows the titular character and friends traveling to an island haven before confronting a mysterious aquatic legend. Counting nationwide previews, the anime has grossed $4.7 million from 604,764 total admissions.

	Gambling crime drama “Tazza: The Song of Beelzebub” placed third in its sophomore frame, taking in $2.2 million from 299,915 admissions across 1,093 screens for an 18% market share. Directed by Choi Kook-hee and starring Byun Yo-han, Noh Jae-won, and Ayaka Miyoshi, the fourth installment in the comic-adapted franchise has grossed $10.2 million from 1,365,648 viewers since its Sep. 23 rollout.
	

	“The Odyssey” took fourth place in its ninth frame, drawing $1.2 million from 123,059 admissions across 678 screens. Its local gross reached $101.2 million from 11,998,236 ticket buyers, leaving the film just under 2,000 admissions shy of the 12-million-ticket threshold.

	Action fantasy “Reawakened Man” opened in fifth place, earning $885,217 from 115,894 admissions across 830 screens. Directed by Baek Seung-ryong and adapted from the popular webtoon, the feature stars Koo Kyo-hwan as a job-seeker who discovers he resurrects three days after dying, using his ability to battle criminal syndicates. Since its mid-week premiere on Sep. 30, the film has taken $1.4 million from 189,802 viewers.

	Auteur Lee Chang-dong’s Venice award winner “Possible Love” took sixth place, grossing $482,385 from 60,534 admissions across 202 screens. Starring Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Cho Yeo-jeong, and Zo In-sung, South Korea’s official international feature film submission has earned $1.7 million from 230,483 admissions since Sep. 23.

	“Obsession” moved to seventh place with $283,437 from 33,886 admissions across 314 screens for a cumulative haul of $7.3 million from 916,738 viewers.

	Warner Bros. Korea comedy remake “The Intern” placed eighth, generating $265,015 from 33,491 admissions across 502 screens. Directed by Kim Do-young and starring Choi Min-sik and Han So-hee, the comedy has accumulated $6.1 million from 834,866 admissions since Sep. 16.

	“Digger” opened in ninth place with $222,627 from 27,580 admissions across 517 screens, lifting its cume to $234,385 from 28,551 viewers following its Oct. 3 bow. 

	Rounding out the top 10, “Avengers: Endgame Encore” took 10th place with $242,747 from 25,777 admissions across 116 screens, bringing its cumulative run to $1.3 million from 148,743 admissions.

	The overall market collective gross for the weekend was $12.6 million, down from last week’s holiday high of $19.6 million.

schema.headline: Korea Box Office: ‘The Assassin(s)’ Holds Admissions Lead as ‘Chiikawa’ Generates Top Weekend Gross

body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Peacock subscribers were hit with another rate hike over the summer, with prices for the NBCUniversal streaming service rising for the fourth time in four years. The price hike came on the heels of Peacock dumping its free trial for new users, joining the ranks of rival streamers like Paramount+, Hulu and HBO Max, all of whom also got rid of their free trial offers.

	But there’s now a way to score a discount on Peacock, as well as take advantage of a free trial, though you’ll have to look elsewhere to claim the latter. Amazon is currently offering a 7-day free trial to Peacock through its Prime Channels hub.


	The deal gets you access to Peacock Premium Plus for free for one week if you sign up through Amazon. Premium Plus is the ad-free streaming tier of Peacock, and now costs $19.99/month (up from $16.99/month earlier this year).

	You won’t be able to find the free trial deal on the Peacock website. With the Prime Channels deal though, you can test drive the service for a week for free, with unlimited access to the entire on-demand library of TV shows and movies, as well as hundreds of hours of live sports streaming. 

	Though there isn’t a catch per se, the Peacock free trial offer is only open to Amazon Prime members (not a Prime member? Get a 30-day free trial here to claim the Peacock deal and get access to exclusive member discounts just in time for Prime Big Deal Days).

	Sign in with your Prime member details and then head to the Prime Video Channels homepage to claim the Peacock free trial offer. Your subscription to Peacock renews at the regular $19.99/month rate after your free trial is up. Or you can cancel at anytime to avoid being charged.

	
		What Are the Best Peacock Streaming Deals 2026?	

	In addition to the Premium Plus plan, Peacock’s latest rate increase brought the price of its Peacock Premium tier (which includes ads) to $12.99/month, up from $10.99/month previously. Its Peacock Select tier, meantime (which includes current and past seasons of select TV shows, but excludes movies, live sports and Peacock originals) jumped from $7.99 to $8.99/month. 

	Still, there’s a way to score a discount on a Peacock subscription. The streamer is offering an annual plan discount right now that gets you 12 months of access for the price of ten.

	The total price is $129 and locks in access for an entire year. That saves you 17% versus paying for Peacock month to month. The limited-time offer is available to all new and eligible returning subscribers and there is no promo code needed.

	Peacock has priced its annual subscription down to as low as $79.99 a year in the past, but with the streamer being home to the recent Olympics and Super Bowl this year, it was able to raise its prices to bring in audiences for the sporting events and it’s unlikely we’ll see a further discount from the current promotion live online.
	
		How to Get Peacock for Free	

	In addition to the Prime Channels free trial offer mentioned above, you can get Peacock for free with a Walmart+ membership. Walmart+ costs $98/year and as part of your membership, members can choose between Peacock Premium or Paramount+ Essential at no added cost.

	That’s in addition to perks like free shipping, free grocery delivery, special discounts, gas savings and more. Sign up for Walmart+ here (you can also test-drive the service for 30 day for just $1 here).

	You can also stream Peacock online for free with Instacart+. The grocery delivery service offers an upgraded tier that gets members free grocery delivery, free restaurant delivery and an annual membership to Peacock for free. Instacart+ costs just $9.99/month or $99/year. Try it out with a 14-day free trial here.

	Peacock is also home to hundreds of new movies such as “Obsession,” “F1” and “The Super Mario Galaxy Movie” plus fan-favorite shows like “Pluribus,” “New Girl,” “The Traitors” “The Office” and the Bravo universe franchises.

	Peacock is also a top-choice streamer for sports fans, who can live stream live sports like the NFL, Premier League, Big Ten Football, and WWE.

title: What David Zaslav Got Wrong About ‘Coyote vs. Acme’
description: Three years after “Coyote vs. Acme” was shelved by Warner Bros. as a tax write-off and rescued by indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment, the Loone
body:
Three years after “Coyote vs. Acme” was shelved by Warner Bros. as a tax write-off and rescued by indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment, the Looney Tunes comedy has become a box-office bright spot with more than $100 million globally. Was Warner Bros. Discovery chief David Zaslav, who deemed it financially unworthy to release on the big screen, wrong to axe the film?

	That answer might depend on who is doing the accounting, analysts say. “Coyote vs. Acme” is a major win for Ketchup Entertainment, which paid $50 million for distribution rights and pre-sold foreign territories to offset the cost. Those grosses might not have been as celebratory for Warner Bros., considering the film cost $70 million to produce. (Theater owners get to keep half of ticket sales.) Warner Bros. dumped the live-action animation hybrid, starring Will Forte and John Cena and produced by DC Studios co-chief James Gunn, for a $30 million tax write-down.
	

	There’s an argument to be made that Warner Bros. would have been able to put more marketing dollars behind the release, which could have elevated global ticket sales. There’s another case that moviegoers rallied behind “Coyote vs. Acme” to prove the studio wrong. By comparison, “Coyote vs. Acme” dramatically outperformed another recent Ketchup-distributed Looney Tunes adventure, 2024’s “The Day the Earth Blew Up: A Looney Tunes Movie,” after Warner Bros. Discovery quietly decided to offload that film as well. “The Day the Earth Blew Up,” whose target audience skewed much younger, grossed $15.4 million globally.
	

	“It’s easy to opine on a decision after we’ve seen the effects,” says Shawn Robbins, founder of Box Office Theory and director of movie analytics at Fandango. “The movie did well partly because of rallying from fans. But it turned out to be a good movie.”

	Buoyed by great reviews and positive word of mouth, “Coyote vs. Acme” launched in late August and started strong with $15.9 million domestically. Ticket sales have since climbed to $59.8 million domestically and $42 million overseas, underscoring the value of PG-rated films with brand familiarity. Theater owners frequently complain that they don’t have enough new movies aimed at families. And while original animation has struggled in post-COVID years, remakes, spinoffs and sequels in kid-friendly franchises, such as “Sonic the Hedgehog” and “PAW Patrol,” have been reliable as modest box office draws.

	The success of “Coyote vs. Acme” is especially glaring given Warner Bros.’ abysmal 2026 box-office performance. The studio has siphoned off a string of money losers, including Tom Cruise’s dark comedy “Digger,” Maggie Gyllenhaal’s punk rock “The Bride!” and DC’s “Supergirl.”

	“There was legacy value in that IP, and the box office grosses of ‘Coyote vs. Acme’ reflect it,” says analyst David A. Gross of FranchiseRe. “All-audience films are extremely valuable and among the biggest earners at the box office. And there would have been upside with stronger marketing.”

	Moreover, the wall-to-wall negative press that Zaslav generated for shelving a finished movie (which was supposedly well received in test screenings) wasn’t worth the headache, according to studio sources. The decision did little to endear the former television executive to the film community after his predecessor Jason Kilar’s ill-fated decision to put the studio’s 2021 slate simultaneously in theaters and on HBO Max had isolated many creatives in Hollywood. Although other employees within Warner Bros. pushed back on the decision to bury the film, Zaslav relegated the final call to accountants, sources add.

	At the time, “Coyote vs. Acme” was the third casualty of Zaslav’s post-pandemic cost-cutting efforts. In 2022, he shocked Hollywood by shelving the $90 million DC-centric “Batgirl” and kid-friendly “Scoob! Holiday Haunt” for tax purposes. Those three films were greenlit by Kilar, the studio’s former chief who departed earlier that year. Zaslav, who succeeded Kilar, said at the time he was shifting the studio’s priorities back to theatrical and felt “Coyote vs. Acme” didn’t fit with the new creative direction of the company. Zaslav’s decision had box office watchers wondering whether the new boss understood the value of the Warner Bros. catalog. After all, “Coyote vs. Acme,” “Batgirl” and “Scoob” hail from well-known brands. And there’s a reason that studios invest so heavily in recognizable franchises – they’re designed to turn the kind of easy profits that help justify other original swings.
	

	“We see so many remakes and sequels because they make money,” says Robbins. “The fact that ‘Coyote vs. Acme’ was based on IP plays into the curiosity behind Warner Bros. [getting rid of it].”

schema.headline: What David Zaslav Got Wrong About ‘Coyote vs. Acme’

title: Marvel Canceled ‘Blade,’ But the Gory Vampire Brawler ‘Half’ Will Thrill Genre Fans
description: Marvel mastermind Kevin Feige has made some of the shrewdest financial decisions in Hollywood history, but he sure dropped the bag when he didn’t ma
body:
Marvel mastermind Kevin Feige has made some of the shrewdest financial decisions in Hollywood history, but he sure dropped the bag when he didn’t make a new “Blade.” (Just ask would-be star Mahershala Ali.)

	Luckily, Indian auteur Samjad has directed a film that will bring joy to fans of the battle-ready half-vampire Wesley Snipes popularized on the big screen. Samjad’s new movie “Half,” which he co-wrote with Praveen Viswanath, has a simple concept: Twin siblings (Ranjith Sajeev and Aiswarya Raj) are robbed and left for dead on a highway, but as they are half-vampires, they recover and vow to take gruesome revenge on the gang that attacked them. From there, the film is a fantasia of blood and gore, as “The Raid 2” and “The Night Comes for Us” fight coordinator Very Tri Yulisman orchestrates creative, funny and bone-crunching action.
	

	Samjad enjoys “Blade,” but had a different vision in mind for his film.


	“What if we take a classic vampire action thriller and execute it in a completely raw, grounded way without a single frame of slow motion?” he says. “That core idea felt so much fresher and visually exciting to me.”

	“Half” has been a powder keg for audiences, resulting in high-energy screenings at its TIFF Midnight Madness debut and at Fantastic Fest. It’s a brawler where the action is clear, crisp and often shot in the daytime. And while the fights feel modern, the film evokes more classic fare.

	“We tried to make the film look like it was shot on an old camera in the olden way, with the old equipment and hard work,” Samjad says. “I think we have to work really hard to get one special shot, right? Now we can achieve it through robotic cams and specialized equipment. Everything is there. But in the olden days, it had to be done through manual hands and panning and zooming. We used lots of zoom lenses because I like the technique with the camera. We tried to achieve the ’80s- and ’90s-type of movie.”
	

	Despite the zippy feature it created, when Samjad describes the “Half” shoot, it’s clear it was a miracle it got made.

	“We were shooting in the middle of a desert,” he says. “It would be a very sunny day, and the heat would go up to 56 Celsius (132.8 Fahrenheit). We can barely stand in the sun. But suddenly everything will change, and clouds will come in, and in 10 to 15 minutes, rain will start and flood everywhere. We put a small shop set near a highway, and when we were shooting, we checked the weather on the internet, and everything was perfect. But suddenly a hailstorm took away all the set, including our tripods, including everything. We faced this every time we shot.”

	Weather wasn’t the only challenge, as a literal war broke out during production.

	“10 days of shooting were finished,” he says. “On the 11th day, there was a war going on, the India and Pakistan war. We had to go back to our home in Keralam [a state in southwestern India]. We were stuck in the middle of the desert, and we suddenly went to our rooms and were evacuated from there, but there was no vehicle, and we could see the missiles and everything going in the sky. We were in a dangerous situation, and somehow with our production’s help, we came back to our home. After the war finished, we went back to the same place and started shooting again after two months.”

	Despite the challenges, Samjad says he was thrilled to play with vampire mythology and had the freedom to do so due to his protagonists’ half-vampire status.

	“There is a healing factor for both of them, as normal vampires have the healing factor,” he says. “As they are half-vampires, we have done something special for them. We can do anything. That’s the power of half-vampires. Our half-vampire could be anything. When they heal, if there is sunlight, the healing will not happen. If there is no sunlight or there is a shadow, healing happens. Normal vampires, when they are exposed to the sun, will burn, right? But half-vampires will not burn, but the healing factor will not work. That’s the idea. We researched vampires, and in India, there are vampire stories from olden days. There were ’70s, ’80s, old black-and-white movies. We have vampires, but in different names. So we took some elements from the European side and mixed up everything.”
	

	“Half” is set to play at the upcoming Sitges Film Festival and is still seeking U.S. distribution.

title: Sarah Jessica Parker Says She’s ‘Never’ Worn Her Archived ‘Sex and the City’ Wardrobe: ‘There’s a Huge Separation Between Myself and Carrie Bradshaw’
description: Despite Carrie Bradshaw’s reputation for wearing trend-setting outfits, Sarah Jessica Parker never wears any of her “Sex and the City” character’s i
body:
Despite Carrie Bradshaw’s reputation for wearing trend-setting outfits, Sarah Jessica Parker never wears any of her “Sex and the City” character’s iconic wardrobe. But she does have it.

	“No, I don’t wear any of the wardrobe that I wore on the show ever. I have it. It’s an archive, but I never wear it. I never have,” Parker told People in a recent interview. 


	For Parker, these one-of-a-kind outfits would feel too much like a costume, especially since they’ve already seen the screen. “There’s a huge separation between myself and Carrie Bradshaw. So it would be like walking around in Sarah Sanderson’s costume,” she continued, referencing her “Hocus Pocus” role. “It doesn’t seem applicable to my life.”
	

	While Bradshaw has laid the character’s wardrobe to rest, she dressed as Bradshaw in the HBO series from 1998 to 2004. Parker revisited the role for two films and the spinoff series, “And Just Like That…,” from 2021 to 2025. Now, audiences have officially said goodbye to Bradshaw and all her iconic outfits. Parker bid her character an emotional farewell on social media when the spinoff ended.

	“Carrie Bradshaw has dominated my professional heartbeat for 27 years. I think I have loved her most of all,” Parker wrote. “I know others have loved her just as I have. Been frustrated, condemned and rooted for her. The symphony of all those emotions has been the greatest soundtrack and most consequential companion. Therefore the most sentimental and profound gratitude and lifetime of debt. To you all.”

	Parker added: “This chapter is complete” and called “And Just Like That” a “joy, adventure, the greatest kind of hard work alongside the most extraordinary talent of 380 that includes all the brilliant actors who joined us.”

schema.headline: Sarah Jessica Parker Says She’s ‘Never’ Worn Her Archived ‘Sex and the City’ Wardrobe: ‘There’s a Huge Separation Between Myself and Carrie Bradshaw’

title: Is ‘Rubber Soul’ the Beatles’ Best Album? The Answer to That is as Malleable as the Shifting Track Lists, but This ‘Super Deluxe’ Is Super Essential: Boxed Set Review
description: What is the Beatles‘ best album? “The one you’re listening to right now” is always the correct answer, of course, and that could encompass “Meet the
body:
What is the Beatles‘ best album? “The one you’re listening to right now” is always the correct answer, of course, and that could encompass “Meet the Beatles” or “Let It Be” at any given moment. But for most fans who aren’t just being sentimental about their first point of entry, it’s usually going to come down to a pick among five — “Rubber Soul,” “Revolver,” “Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band,” “The Beatles” and “Abbey Road” — with the first-mentioned there sometimes being the last-cited, because that 1965 transitional LP isn’t as fully ambitious in scope as those that followed. “Rubber Soul” is undoubtedly among the most influential albums ever released, make no mistake. Yet it was arguably the last Beatles record (at least until “Let It Be”) that was tossed off reasonably casually, on deadline, and not consciously aiming at being some kind of tour de force.
	

	Which is partly why I’ve suddenly joined the stubborn minority flank of fans that has always thought of “Rubber Soul” as the best all-around effort. That could change in 15 minutes, naturally, because it happens to be The One I’m Listening To Right Now — in its very expanded form as “Rubber Soul: Special Edition Super Deluxe,” a five-LP or four-CD set that finally reached the world Friday after many years of fans’ wishing and hoping. Or it might be 15 months before I switch sides on this one and go back to the White Album. Because there’s something about “Rubber Soul” in all of its released forms, including the substantially different original U.K. and U.S. versions, that makes for the Fabs’ most consistent listening experience.
	

	It provided — provides — a different kind of joy than the kind of whiplash that the world would get when the screaming guitar of “Taxman” gave way to borrowing the “Psycho” strings to mourn all the lonely people, and other hilariously sharp juxtapositions on “Revolver” going forward. “Rubber Soul,” in contrast, catches the Beatles constantly at the glorious nexus of rocking and mature. (Or folk-rocking, but the force of the electric guitar remains strong.) It’s kind of the last bastion of Carl Perkins’ influence being stronger than the pot’s, but with the looming spectres of Dylan, the Byrds and Simon & Garfunel getting also getting their licks in before the psychedelia, orchestration and music-hall homages seriously creep in.

	And it’s the sound of the Beatles almost accidentally catching lightning in a bottle, before they more deliberately put their kites way, way up in the air for just about everything that followed. There’s a shorter way to describe it: perfect.

	The boxed set has four distinct components, each of them incredibly necessary, whether new or old: the requisite fresh stereo remix of the U.K. album from Giles Martin and Sam Okell; a collection of studio outtakes; the U.K. track list in mono, revisited; and the American version in stereo. So, in order not just of appearance, but of what you need:

	The first thing to know is that the remix is essential… and compared to the boxed set, it can be had for cheap — free, really, in these days of streaming — and so there is little excuse to not give this piece a chance. Not surprisingly, the Beatles’ mass fandom has had mixed, if primarily positive, thoughts about past Martin/Okell full-album remixes, but it’s difficult to imagine there being very many souls out there who will not regard this as a spectacular upgrade, any passing sonic quibbles aside. No Beatles album stood in more need of their touch, arguably. When George Martin previously took a whack at a new mix, he remained largely reverent toward the panning that was done to put “Soul” in stereo in the ’60s. Revisiting that approach in the U.S. stereo reprisal here is still fun, in a quaint way: You are right in the studio with the Beatles — and half of them are on one side of you and half are on the other! But only the most perverse among us would maintain that ultra-separation is how “Rubber Soul” ought to remain forever, much less was intended as an essential part of its conception. The fresh mix is far from radical, but achieves its mission of making the album sound relevant to the ears of 2026 and 2086, while fooling you into thinking it’s just the way you’ve always heard it for years.
	

	Some of us will leap to the cutting-room-floor section, which has 26 unreleased scraps — none of it completely revelatory, all of it a pleasure to listen to for anyone who knows the finsihed recordings by heart. Vocals and instrumental tracks were typically recorded separately at this time, so we get a lot of backing-tracks-in-progress before the lead vox and harmonies were overlaid, but there are a handful of actual demos or early scrub takes that survived being erased. Plus one never-before-reported tune that apparently surfaced only recently, a couple of minutes of a John Lennon demo of “Little Girl,” a modest charmer that probably would have seemed too impossibly old-fashioned for “Rubber Soul,” even fleshed out. It would be lying to say the world was any worse for having been denied this Lennon curio till now. But as the capper to a fairly voluminous amount of more familiar works-in-progress, “Little Girl” is a nice dessert.

	Hearing so many isolated instrumental tracks does make for some discoveries that maybe were already obvious to the most attentive Beatles buffs, but might still be surprising to others of us. Like: how much of a borderline-country album “Rubber Soul” was and is. The non-vocal version of “Run for Your Life,” for instance, sounds as much like a Buck Owens track as their cover of “Act Naturally” did on the previous album, and there’s really a good deal of C&W or rockabilly throughout, for a group that was soon to be acid-tripping. You also get a version of “Michelle” with the harmonies turned up so high, it almost sounds like a barbershop-quartet homage. We get to hear “In My Life” without any solo at all, much less the George Martin piano part that was sped up x2 to become a harpichord… but there’s also a short excerpt of a version that tried out an organ solo, recorded by John on a cassette in the control room.

	The most fun outtakes might be the early tries we hear of “Day Tripper” (which was never on any version of “Rubber Soul,” but on a single as part of the same era). There’s a kind of hootenanny-style recording, before the signature riff was composed, and then, once things get electric, we get delightful outtake arrangements where they tried ramping up the intensity in certain parts of the song… plus lots and lots more of the Ringo fills you know and love. And a version of “I’m Looking Through You” that goes on for about 45 seconds longer than the release version, so Beatles fans can hear more of a fairly rare example of Paul being a little mean. Part of the reason “I’m Looking Through You” runs longer in the outtake is because the parts of the song where it wants to turn into a rave-up go on for a few bars longer each time, as if they really wanted to work in a little more of the “soul” sound promised in the title. With “Norwegian Wood,” there’s a progression of different degrees of use of the sitar sound, from a take that has too much of George Harrison‘s use of the exotic instrument — it sounds like it’s about to turn right into “Within You Without You” — to a version with none at all, before they settle on a mixture that’s just right.
	

	Having both the U.K. and U.S. editions represented here in faithful recreations of how those audiences have long heard the album allows the chance to revive the eternal debate of which track listing was better. Americans may have gotten a better idea, faster, of how strong the folk strains were on the album by it beginning with “I’ve Just Seen a Face” (which had already appeared on “Help!” in Europe), leading right into the one-night-stand reportage of “Norwegian Wood.” But of course if you forever heard it as opening with “Drive My Car,” in the U.K. (and not included at all on the U.S. version), your tendency would have been to remember it as a solid rock ‘n’ roll album. In the end, no one loses either way, but it’s fascinating to think about how these perceptions might have been forged differently by some fairly arbitrary choices at the time. Thankfully, we all have the liberty now to take the 16 songs that were included on either or both sides of the pond, add the double-A-side single “Day Tripper”/”We Can Work It Out” (included as a 7-inch single in the vinyl boxed set), and make “Rubber Soul” what it could have been in a perfect world: an 18-song masterpiece without a duff track anywhere in the mix.

	The wild thing is that you can hear all of this for pennies on the dollar through your Spotify or Tidal subscription. What you can’t get, beyond the handsome packaging of the individual LP components, is the hardback coffee table book that offers a wealth of annotation on every one of these 18 songs, along with the bigger-picture perspective on where the Beatles were in this culture where they leading the cultural changing of the guard. It’s hard to imagine living without it, for the recording details but also the reminder of, say, where McCartney was at in his relationship with Jane Asher, and how that led to the hopeful “We Can Work It Out” and not-so-hopeful “I’m Looking Through You,” or whether “Drive My Car” counts in the lineage of the group’s “comedy” songs, or whether Lennon meant “Nowhere Man” as an attack on squares or on himself, and the discrepancies between the later accounts of John and Paul — never to be settled, at this late date — over who wrote the melody to “In My Life.”

	All wonderful grist for the Beatlemaniac mill, but at the core of it, a singular yet malleable album that had “rubber” in the title but really put in concrete how much the Beatles would mean to us in the years and millennia to come.

schema.headline: Is ‘Rubber Soul’ the Beatles’ Best Album? The Answer to That is as Malleable as the Shifting Track Lists, but This ‘Super Deluxe’ Is Super Essential: Boxed Set Review

body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	The 2026-27 NFL season is underway, and fans who want to watch the games from home can now take advantage of a Fox One offer, which gets you a free trial to the official Fox streaming service.

	Fox is one of the official television broadcasters for NFL games, in addition to the MLB playoffs and the World Series, and Fox One allows viewers to livestream all of the games that air on Fox without needing cable.


	In addition to the main Fox network, the Fox Corp. streaming platform also includes access to live sports on Fox Sports, FS1, FS2 and Fox Deportes, plus content from Fox News, Fox Business, Fox Weather and BTN, among others. That means viewers can also tune in to college football games from the Big Ten, Big 12, Mountain West, and select games from other partner conferences, plus college basketball, international soccer, motorsports (like NASCAR) and more.

	
		How to Get Fox One App for Free	

	A subscription to Fox One costs $19.99/month but the streamer is offering a limited-time deal that lets you test drive the service for free for three days. That’s enough time to stream a weekend’s worth of sports in addition to all the TV shows and news programming on the Fox networks.

	Your subscription renews at the regular monthly rate of $19.99 after your free trial is over or you can cancel beforehand to avoid being charged.

	If you choose to continue, you can save $3.99/month when you bundle Fox Nation ($8.99/month) with Fox One ($19.99/month). While Fox One is home to live sports and entertainment, Fox Nation gets you on-demand access to the network’s news and talk programming, including shows like “Hannity, “The Five” and true crime originals.


	Both the free trial offer and the bundle deal are available through Amazon’s Prime Channels hub here. The Fox One offers are only available to Amazon Prime members. Not a Prime member? Get a 30-day free trial here.

	You can also get Fox One for free through Fubo, a live TV streaming service that is including access to the Fox One app for free with its Fubo Core package right now. The package also includes access to Fox, Fox Sports, FS1 and FS2, as well as ESPN for post-game highlights and analysis. Fubo’s Pro plan starts as low as $63.99/month (reg. $68.99/month) for your first month of service. Don’t want to commit? Get a five-day free trial to Fubo here.

	DirecTV subscribers can also log into the Fox One app for free without needing to pay for a separate subscription. The cheapest DirecTV plan for watching Fox sports is the streamer’s “MyNews Genre Pack,” which gets you a live Fox feed and 10 other channels for $34.99/month. DirecTV also offers a five-day free trial that you can use to access Fox One online for free.

	Subscribers to Sling can also use their Sling credentials to sign in to the Fox One app for free. Sling doesn’t offer a free trial but has the most affordable streaming packages online, with access to FS1 and Fox (in designated markets) starting at $19.99/month.
